gemstone grading vs diamond grading
a: Gemstone appraisal and grading uses a framework adapted from diamond grading but with important differences because colored stones lack standard market pricing. The primary value factors—often called the 4 Cs for colored stones (Color, Clarity, Cut, Carat weight)—are applied differently: Color is overwhelmingly the most important factor for colored gemstones, evaluated by hue (the primary color—red, blue, green, etc.), tone (lightness to darkness), and saturation (intensity from dull to vivid). For colored stones, clarity is less critical than for diamonds—a perfect ruby with no inclusions is nearly impossible and inclusions (jardin in emerald, silk in ruby) are accepted as natural fingerprints, though the size, number, and visibility of inclusions affect value. Cut quality for colored stones must balance brilliance with color saturation—a very pale stone may be cut deeper to concentrate color (creating a windowed or dark stone), while a very dark stone may be cut shallower to allow more light transmission. Carat weight has a super-exponential price curve (a 5-carat fine ruby costs far more than 5 times a 1-carat ruby) because large high-quality colored stones are rarer than large diamonds. Additional value factors include origin (Burmese rubies, Colombian emeralds, Kashmir sapphires command enormous premiums even when lower-quality specimens from other sources are cheaper), treatment disclosure (untreated stones are typically 50-200% more expensive than heat-treated equivalents, and stones with undisclosed or unstable treatments lose all value), and market trends (demand for specific colors and sources fluctuates with fashion and celebrity influence).

gemological certification labs comparison
a: Gemological certification laboratories provide independent, scientific identification of gemstones and, for some labs, origin determination and treatment disclosure. The Gemological Institute of America (GIA) is the world's most respected gemological laboratory, known for its rigorous diamond grading and colored stone identification reports—GIA colored stone reports provide species identification, weight, measurements, shape/cut, color and clarity grades (using standardized descriptive terminology rather than a letter scale), and treatment disclosure (including whether a stone is natural, synthetic, or simulant, and if any enhancement has been detected). GRS (GemResearch Swisslab) is one of the most recognized labs for colored stone origin determination and heat treatment disclosure, particularly for rubies, sapphires, and emeralds—their reports command confidence in the auction and high-end jewelry trade. SSEF (Swiss Foundation for the Research of Gemstones) is another top-tier lab in Basel, known for emerald, ruby, sapphire, pearl, and jade certification, with advanced testing including EDXRF chemical fingerprinting for origin determination. AIGS (Asian Institute of Gemological Sciences, Bangkok) pioneered colored stone origin determination in Thailand. Gubelin Gem Lab (Lucerne) is the oldest continuous gemological laboratory, renowned for the highest level of expertise and detailed reports. IGI (International Gemological Institute) and EGL (European Gemological Laboratory) are more widely available but have less authority for high-end colored stones. Major auction houses (Sotheby's, Christie's) require reports from at least two reputable labs for important gems, and discrepancies between labs—especially on origin and treatment—are not uncommon and can significantly affect value.

a: Many famous gemstones have legendary histories and immense values. The Hope Diamond (45.52-carat deep blue diamond, Smithsonian) is famous for its dramatic color, phosphorescence (glowing red after UV exposure), and the supposed curse that brought misfortune to its successive owners—it was originally part of the French Blue diamond stolen during the French Revolution and recut. The Koh-i-Noor (Mountain of Light, 105.6 carats, British Crown Jewels) originated in India's Golconda mines and passed through Mughal emperors, Persian invaders, Sikh rulers, and finally the British East India Company—under British law it was controversially ceded to the Crown and has been the subject of repatriation demands from India, Pakistan, and Afghanistan. The Cullinan diamond (3,106 carats rough) is the largest gem-quality diamond ever found, discovered in South Africa in 1905; it was cut into 9 major stones (Cullinan I, the Great Star of Africa at 530 carats in the Sovereign's Sceptre, and Cullinan II in the Imperial State Crown) and 96 smaller brilliants. The Star of India (563-carat star sapphire, American Museum of Natural History) is the largest star sapphire in the world, with extraordinarily well-defined asterism, and was infamously stolen in a 1964 heist (recovered shortly after). The Timur Ruby and Black Prince's Ruby are both actually large red spinels mounted in the British Crown Jewels, mistaken for rubies for centuries. The Logan Sapphire (423 carats, Smithsonian) is one of the largest faceted blue sapphires in existence. Larger historical treasures include the Bahia Emerald (incredibly massive 752-pound rough emerald from Brazil), the Patricia Emerald (632-carat flawless crystal from Colombia), and the Elizabeth Taylor Collection's 33-carat Krupp Diamond and 68-carat Taylor-Burton Diamond.
